title: Argentum Insurance - Private VPC Egress & Firewall Architecture Review
summary: Discovery + security deep dive focused on private VPC deployment topology, ingress/egress controls, firewalling and logging. Customer emphasized strict egress allowlist, keys must remain customer-managed (BYOK), logs sent to internal SIEM over PrivateLink, SOC2/ISO evidence required. Agreed next steps: share architecture diagram, SOC2 package, run egress allowlist pilot, schedule on-prem runbook review.
topics: Firewall rules vs security groups vs NGFW
next_steps: Redwood: send updated architecture diagram and network flow (Maya)
Redwood: share SOC2/ISO artifact bundle and pen-test summary
Argentum: provide initial egress allowlist for pilot
Set up test SIEM forwarding (customer provides endpoint)
action_items: Maya Chen | Send network diagram and packet flow mockup | 2025-06-16
Liam O'Connor | Prepare egress allowlist test plan and recommended proxy config | 2025-06-18
Marco Silva | Provide current VPC CIDR blocks and egress IP inventory | 2025-06-15
Elena Ruiz | Share SOC2 scoping questions and compliance constraints | 2025-06-17
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, account exec on Redwood. We have Liam and Sofia from the engineering side.
[00:00:10] Daniel Park: Hi, Daniel here. I'll be running point at Argentum. Elena, Marco and Priya are on.
[00:00:21] Elena Ruiz: Hey, good to meet you. We're mostly here to validate network isolation and how logs are handled.
[00:00:28] Maya Chen: Great. Agenda is simple: we want to walk through our private VPC architecture and how we enforce ingress/egress and firewalling, talk BYOK/KMS and logging. Liam, you want to kick off with the topology?
[00:00:42] Liam O'Connor: Yeah, sure. I'll try to keep it high level first then dive into specifics. So for a Private deployment, there are two main planes to think about: the data plane, which runs in your VPC or on-prem, and our control plane. For Argentum we recommend a private-control-plane integration model — control plane communicates via a narrow set of egress endpoints over PrivateLink or a dedicated peering channel.
[00:01:07] Marco Silva: Can you clarify "control plane" traffic? We cannot allow arbitrary outbound. Everything has to be scoped to specific IPs or domain names, approved by our network team.
[00:01:16] Liam O'Connor: Absolutely. We provide a fixed set of FQDNs and a small set of egress IP ranges per region. For on-prem or VPC, we support either PrivateLink endpoints (recommended) so nothing traverses the public internet, or if you must egress we can give a static egress IP pool for allowlisting.
[00:01:35] Elena Ruiz: PrivateLink is preferred. What's the authentication for the control plane? We can't have credentials floating on unsecured hosts.
[00:01:41] Sofia Patel: We use mTLS mutual auth for control plane connections. That plus a short-lived credential exchange and attestation. Control plane certs are rotated; you can pin CA roots in your environment.
[00:01:52] Tom Briggs: So the data never hits Redwood public endpoints in the plain internet if we use PrivateLink?
[00:01:57] Liam O'Connor: Correct, no public egress required. Data plane requests to inference models stay in your VPC and only model telemetry/metrics optionally go to the control plane, depending on your config. We can disable telemetry entirely for regulated workloads.
[00:02:12] Daniel Park: Let's drill into egress. We have strict policy: only allow outbound to triaged endpoints via our egress proxy. How does Redwood support that?
[00:02:21] Liam O'Connor: Two models. 1) PrivateLink / VPC endpoint where you never egress publicly. 2) If you run in a network that requires an egress proxy, we recommend routing control plane traffic through your proxy; your proxy can allowlist Redwood egress IPs or FQDNs. We publish an authoritative list and tolerably small changes are announced. For software updates (model weights, container image pulls) we support mirroring repositories to your artifact registry — so you never need outbound access to our mirrors.
[00:02:47] Marco Silva: Mirroring images is important. Do you support offline package delivery for on-prem?
[00:02:51] Liam O'Connor: Yes, we have an on-prem bundle and an offline installer for fully air-gapped installs. That process also includes checksums and signed artifacts.
[00:02:59] Elena Ruiz: Firewalling strategy: do you use security groups and NACLs only or do you integrate with our NGFW (we run Palo Alto)?
[00:03:06] Sofia Patel: We use security groups and subnets as first-line segmentation. For customers with NGFW we integrate fine — our recommendation is to front the data plane with your NGFW and only allow the minimal ports. Typical ports are HTTPS/TCP 443 for control plane, and ephemeral ports for management (SSH/jumpbox) controlled by a bastion in a management subnet.
[00:03:26] Priya Nair: How about ingress? We want no public ingress into the nodes.
[00:03:30] Liam O'Connor: For private deployments we deploy a private load balancer or internal NLB. Your application talks to the local private endpoint. Admin access is via bastion host with MFA and SAML-based SSO.
[00:03:41] Tom Briggs: Regarding bastion — can we force session recording and gateway jump?
[00:03:45] Sofia Patel: Yes, we integrate with your session broker (e.g., Teleport, BastionHost) and can require recorded sessions via your proxy. We also respect your AD/SAML mapping and RBAC.
[00:03:55] Elena Ruiz: Let's talk keys. We need BYOK with HSM-backed keys and customer control for key rotation.
[00:04:02] Liam O'Connor: We offer two modes: Bring-Your-Own-Key via customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS) where data-plane encryption keys are customer-held and used for envelope encryption. For on-prem we integrate with HSMs via PKCS#11 or KMIP. Keys never leave your KMS/HSM. Redwood only receives wrapped keys with limited usage tokens.
[00:04:25] Daniel Park: Can you do attestation or provide audit proof that keys were never exported?
[00:04:29] Rajiv Menon: We can provide KMS/HSM access logs with a cryptographic trail; we also surface key usage metrics in the console and in audit log exports. For HSMs, our connector only performs unwrap operations and logs them to the audit stream.
[00:04:40] Elena Ruiz: About encryption at rest for model artifacts and cache — we need to ensure S3 buckets can't be read by Redwood engineers directly.
[00:04:47] Sofia Patel: If you control the KMS keys, access is enforced by IAM policies and KMS grants. We can also run the storage in your account so you're the principal on the buckets; Redwood's service role is scoped by assumption roles and requires explicit sts:AssumeRole with MFA.
[00:05:03] Marco Silva: That seems ok. Now audit logs — how do we get runtime logs into our Splunk stack without going over the internet?
[00:05:10] Liam O'Connor: We support log forwarding over syslog/TLS to your SIEM via PrivateLink or peering. For cloud customers we can place a log forwarder into your VPC that pushes to your SIEM endpoint over private connectivity. Logs are structured JSON, include request_id, model_id, latency, and a redaction marker for PII which you can configure.
[00:05:34] Priya Nair: We need log retention controls and the ability to delete logs on request for data subject requests.
[00:05:39] Sofia Patel: You control log retention; logs are stored in your account/VPC. If you prefer Redwood-managed storage, we provide retention TTLs and a delete API with an auditable trail.
[00:05:50] Elena Ruiz: SOC 2 and ISO — we'll need evidence and an AICPA report, plus encryption scope. What artifacts can you share?
[00:05:59] Maya Chen: We can share our SOC2 Type II report, ISO 27001 certificate, pen test summary, and our internal security controls mapping. We'll redact customer-specific PII but provide evidence of controls. We'll send the artifact bundle after an NDA or via our secure artifact share.
[00:06:13] Daniel Park: Can you map controls to our internal policy numbers? We have a compliance matrix.
[00:06:18] Maya Chen: Yes — we typically do a control mapping spreadsheet (we map our controls to SOC2/ISO and can map to your policy IDs). We'll also do a scoping call with your compliance team.
[00:06:27] Marco Silva: One operational concern: worker nodes will occasionally reach out for OS package updates. We require package mirrors internally.
[00:06:34] Liam O'Connor: We recommend customers mirror package repositories into their artifact registry and block outbound. We also support locked base images and regular signed updates you can pull from your registry.
[00:06:45] Tom Briggs: On firewall rules specifics — can you provide a list of ports and domains that need to be allowed for a minimal deployment?
[00:06:51] Liam O'Connor: Yes — we'll produce a minimal egress/ingress spreadsheet. For the minimal control plane connectivity you need HTTPS to our control-plane FQDNs and access to STS endpoints for token exchange if using IAM roles. If using PrivateLink, it's just the endpoint service and no public ports.
[00:07:07] Elena Ruiz: About network segmentation: we want separate subnets for inference and model management. Any recommended best practices?
[00:07:12] Sofia Patel: Definitely. Put inference nodes in isolated private subnets with no route to internet gateway. Put model management and build systems in a separate subnet with NAT and strict egress. Use security groups to limit traffic between subnets and your NGFW to enforce deep packet inspection on the management plane.
[00:07:29] Priya Nair: What about KV cache artifacts — are those stored encrypted and in our account?
[00:07:33] Liam O'Connor: Cache storage can live in your tenancy; it's encrypted with your keys. If you prefer ephemeral in-memory cache only, we can disable persistent KV cache.
[00:07:42] Marco Silva: Let's surface the threat model around data leakage via telemetry — what telemetry do you collect by default?
[00:07:48] Rajiv Menon: By default we collect performance telemetry and anonymized error traces. For regulated customers we offer opt-out of telemetry and only collect minimal health pings. We also have a prompt redaction layer that can be configured to strip PII before any optional telemetry leaves the VPC.
[00:08:05] Elena Ruiz: How robust is RBAC and SSO integration? We have requirement for SCIM-based provisioning and SAML 2.0.
[00:08:12] Sofia Patel: We support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with the ability to create custom roles and map SAML groups to roles. All admin actions are audited and visible in the audit log.
[00:08:25] Tom Briggs: Are there emergency access procedures if the control plane is unreachable? Can we continue inference locally?
[00:08:30] Liam O'Connor: Yes. We support a fail-open mode for critical workloads where inference continues against a pinned model snapshot locally. Control plane features (metrics, rollouts) will be unavailable, but inference maintains service. This is configurable per deployment.
[00:08:44] Daniel Park: That addresses availability. One more: vulnerability management and patching cadence?
[00:08:49] Rajiv Menon: We publish a quarterly CVE bulletin and critical patches are pushed as needed. For Private/on-prem, customers can opt into managed patching or self-managed. All changes go through a canary and rollout process.
[00:08:59] Marco Silva: Good. Let's talk about egress allowlist pilot logistics.
[00:09:04] Maya Chen: Liam, can you summarize what we'll provide for the pilot?
[00:09:07] Liam O'Connor: We'll provide: 1) a minimal egress/FQDN and port list, 2) recommended proxy config example (squid/nginx forward proxy) and a small test harness that simulates control plane calls, 3) a checklist for PrivateLink vs static IP allowlist decisions.
[00:09:24] Marco Silva: And a timeline? We'd like to run the pilot in our dev VPC next week.
[00:09:28] Maya Chen: We'll aim to get the packet to you within 48 hours and then we can schedule a 90-minute run-through with your NetOps.
[00:09:35] Elena Ruiz: Regarding evidence for SOC2: we'll need the Type II report and the pen-test results. Also, do you have a third-party attestation for supply chain security?
[00:09:44] Maya Chen: We do have a software SBOM process and can share high-level SBOM artifacts; for full supply chain attestation we use Signed Build pipelines and can describe that process in detail in the docs.
[00:09:58] Tom Briggs: Any gotchas around NAT gateways and ephemeral egress IP churn?
[00:10:02] Liam O'Connor: Yes — if you rely on NAT gateway IPs that can change during autoscaling or AZ failover. We recommend using egress NAT with Elastic IPs or using PrivateLink to avoid that problem.
[00:10:13] Elena Ruiz: Do you support peered VPCs for model storage — e.g., models stored in a central S3 in another account?
[00:10:18] Sofia Patel: Yes — we support cross-account roles and VPC peering. Best practice is to keep model artifact storage in the same account as the data plane to simplify IAM scoping, but peering works with proper IAM trust.
[00:10:31] Daniel Park: Ok, sounds like we have a plan. Let's capture next steps.
[00:10:35] Maya Chen: Recap: We'll send diagrams, SOC2/ISO artifacts, egress allowlist doc, and schedule the pilot and runbook review. Anything I'm missing?
[00:10:44] Elena Ruiz: Please include the signed offline installer checklist for air-gapped installs.
[00:10:48] Maya Chen: Will do. Thanks all — we'll follow up via the CRM.
[00:10:54] Daniel Park: Thanks everyone.
[00:10:57] [end of recording]
questions: Can Redwood support BYOK with HSM integration?
Is PrivateLink sufficient to avoid public internet egress for control plane?
What telemetry does Redwood collect by default and can it be disabled?
